rationale: B wins because it keeps the four sellable lanes clean: money, moat, driver, connector. A has good bones in "A not-yet-profitable EV maker opens its chargers to rivals' customers and calls it a revenue stream," but then drifts into unsupported theater with "After Tesla" and "Wall Street hasn't repriced it yet." B's "Rivian's new stalls will speak both plugs — CCS and NACS on every one" is a sharper fourth angle than A's proprietary-era obituary because it gives a real infrastructure reporter a concrete decision to test.
gaps_in_A: "After Tesla, Rivian opens its charging network to all EVs" imports a Tesla Supercharger comparison that was not in the supplied update. That is outside-context scaffolding, not grounding.
"The proprietary-charger era is fading" is a trend verdict built from one provided company announcement. Too much gravitas, not enough evidence.
"Wall Street hasn't repriced it yet" invents a market reaction. No stock move, analyst note, or valuation data was supplied.
"what charging revenue could move the needle" uses blacklisted PR sludge and ducks the real question: materiality against Rivian's losses.
gaps_in_B: "capital-heavy cost center" is plausible, but it is still an inferred accounting frame. The supplied facts say chargers exist and utilization should improve; they do not prove cost-center economics.
"Every other EV driver" overstates the consumer angle until compatibility, geography, and activation details are verified.

"the rest of the industry still holds" turns the moat angle a little too grand. The update supports Rivian choosing utilization revenue over exclusivity; it does not prove what the whole industry believes.
